setupSteps: Wall choice: a flat, firm wall with nothing hanging on it and no sockets or switches at back height. Avoid freshly painted or damp walls.
Floor: a non-slip floor. If your socks slip, wear shoes with grip or barefoot on a mat. Do not use a mat that can slide.
Back position: stand with your back, hips and shoulders touching the wall. The head can touch the wall lightly.

Foot position: walk your feet forward about 60 cm (two feet, est.) from the wall, hip-width to shoulder-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead or turned out only slightly. The farther forward the feet are, the more the knees stay behind the toes (commonly taught; the research behind the "knees behind toes" rule is limited, so treat it as a coaching cue).

Arms: let your hands hang by your sides, or fold them across your chest. Do not push your hands down on your thighs (this takes load off the legs and can hide poor depth) and do not rest your hands on your knees.
Camera: place the phone at hip height about 2 m (est.) to your side, so shoulder, hip, knee and ankle are all in the frame.
Clothing: fitted leggings or track pants and a fitted top so the camera can see the knees and hips. Loose kurtas or dupattas hide the knee line.
Timer and water: have a visible clock or use the app timer. Keep a bottle nearby.
Blood pressure check: if you have high blood pressure or heart disease, read section 9 before the first hold.

steps.part: A. Shallow beginner wall sit (about 130-140 degree knee angle, hold 15-30 s)
steps.title: Stand with your back to the wall
steps.action: Stand tall with shoulders, hips and back lightly touching the wall, feet hip-width apart.
steps.feel: Even weight through both feet; shoulders relaxed.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder, hip and ankle in one vertical line. Front: shoulders level, feet hip-width apart.

steps.part: A. Shallow beginner wall sit (about 130-140 degree knee angle, hold 15-30 s)
steps.title: Walk the feet forward
steps.action: Take small steps forward until your feet are about 60 cm (est.) from the wall, then put your back against the wall again.
steps.feel: Back and hips in light contact with the wall.
steps.visualCheck: Side: feet clearly in front of the hips. Front: feet parallel and level.

steps.part: A. Shallow beginner wall sit (about 130-140 degree knee angle, hold 15-30 s)
steps.title: Slide down a little
steps.action: Bend your knees and slide down the wall only about 10-15 cm (est.) so the knees bend about 40-50 degrees. Stop there.
steps.feel: Mild work in the front of the thighs. No pain in the kneecap or lower back.
steps.breathing: Breathe out gently as you slide.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees clearly behind the toes, thigh well above horizontal. Front: knees over the second toe, not falling inward.

steps.part: A. Shallow beginner wall sit (about 130-140 degree knee angle, hold 15-30 s)
steps.title: Hold and breathe
steps.action: Stay still with your back on the wall, weight through the whole foot.
steps.feel: Thigh muscles working harder, maybe a mild burn late in the hold.
steps.breathing: Slow in through the nose and out through the mouth; never hold your breath (talk or count aloud if you tend to hold it).
steps.visualCheck: Side: depth does not change; head stays level. Front: both knees stay the same distance apart.

steps.part: A. Shallow beginner wall sit (about 130-140 degree knee angle, hold 15-30 s)
steps.title: Slide up
steps.action: Press through the whole foot and slide up the wall until the legs are straight, or follow the Cleveland Clinic exit: bring one foot back toward the wall and slide up.
steps.feel: Thighs relax; knees do not click.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back sliding up the wall, not bouncing.

steps.part: A. Shallow beginner wall sit (about 130-140 degree knee angle, hold 15-30 s)
steps.title: Rest
steps.action: Step away from the wall and shake your legs out.
steps.visualCheck: Stop for the day if the hold felt shaky or you felt dizzy.

steps.part: B. Quarter wall sit (knee angle about 120 degrees, est.)
steps.title: Same setup. Slide down until the knees bend about 60 degrees (knee angle about 120, est.). The thighs are well above level

steps.part: B. Quarter wall sit (knee angle about 120 degrees, est.)
steps.title: Hold 20-45 s with steady breathing. Stop at once if the front of the knee hurts

steps.part: C. Parallel wall sit (knee angle about 90-100 degrees)
steps.title: Same setup, but walk the feet far enough that the knees sit over the ankles at the bottom and the thighs are level with the floor (sources describe hips, knees and ankles at about 90 degrees)

steps.part: C. Parallel wall sit (knee angle about 90-100 degrees)
steps.title: Hold 30-60 s or longer. Only when you can hold the quarter version cleanly for 45 s (est.)

commonMistakes.title: Going too deep too soon
commonMistakes.text: Going too deep too soon. Why: deep holds are much harder, and kneecap pressure rises sharply past about 90 degrees of knee bend (fit-pro column, not a trial). Fix: start shallow and add depth only after clean holds.

commonMistakes.title: Knees too far forward over the toes
commonMistakes.text: Knees too far forward over the toes. Why: a common coaching cue says it loads the knee more and the thighs less (limited research). Fix: walk the feet forward so the shins are near upright and the knees stay behind the toes.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding raises blood pressure more than open breathing during effort (lab data from heavy lifting, PubMed 7741618), and wall sits are isometric. Fix: slow breaths in and out, count aloud.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing hands on the thighs
commonMistakes.text: Pushing hands on the thighs. Why: it takes load off the legs and can hide poor depth. Fix: arms by the sides or folded.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving in
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving in. Why: poor knee alignment is a common cue in every guide. Fix: push the knees out over the middle toes; if they still cave, slide up a little.

commonMistakes.title: Heels lifting or weight on the toes
commonMistakes.text: Heels lifting or weight on the toes. Why: the thighs lose their base. Fix: heels down, feet flat.

commonMistakes.title: Back peeling off the wall or leaning forward
commonMistakes.text: Back peeling off the wall or leaning forward. Why: the trunk is meant to rest, and leaning shifts the load. Fix: shoulders, hips and back touch the wall; shorten the hold.

commonMistakes.title: Calling a high sit a full one without tracking depth
commonMistakes.text: Calling a high sit a full one without tracking depth. Why: a sit that is too high is a valid beginner rung but is not the same as parallel. Fix: name the depth (shallow, quarter, parallel) and film from the side.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing through pain
commonMistakes.text: Pushing through pain. Why: sharp front-knee or back pain means the depth is too much (several guides advise stopping). Fix: slide up, rest, and use a shallower depth.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing the exit
commonMistakes.text: Rushing the exit. Why: dropping to the floor or springing up can jolt the knees and cause dizziness. Fix: slide up slowly with palms or one foot back, and rise slowly if you feel light-headed.

safetyNotes: High blood pressure and heart disease: isometric holds raise blood pressure while you hold, especially with breath-holding. Mayo Clinic advises checking with a provider before isometric exercise if you have high blood pressure or heart problems, and never to hold your breath or strain. Harvard Health advises breathing normally, with a big breath before the hold rather than straining. Use short, shallow, light holds, breathe throughout, rise slowly, and do not stop prescribed medicines. Severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure needs medical clearance first.
Knee problems: deep holds can irritate the front of the knee. Stay above the painful depth (a partial wall sit around 45 degrees knee bend, est.) and stop for sharp pain, swelling or locking.
Lower back problems: the back is supported by the wall, but stop if pain grows or spreads down a leg.
Pregnancy and postpartum: ask your doctor; use a ball or wall variation only with approval; lying or standing still can cause dizziness; stop for bleeding, pain or contractions.
Dizziness, balance problems, recent surgery: only with approval and with a wall and a clear space.
